title: Confirmation Bias — AI is The Ultimate Thinking Machine? Or a Syntax Calculator?
excerpt: A study published in the Harvard Business Review confirmed what many suspected: LLM models don't analyse your problem — they confirm your hypotheses. The variable that most influenced strategic recommendations was not context, nor prompt quality. It was the order in which options were presented.
content:
Published on LinkedIn Pulse, 7 June 2026.

A study published in March 2026 at the Harvard Business Review confirmed what many had suspected, but few had managed to prove with rigour: large language models — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and others — do not analyse a given problem. They confirm the hypotheses provided.

The cited research tested over 15,000 distinct scenarios, covering seven classic strategic tensions in business: differentiation vs. commoditisation, automation vs. augmentation, short-term vs. long-term, radical vs. incremental innovation, centralisation vs. decentralisation, competition vs. collaboration, exploration vs. exploitation. For each tension, the researchers systematically varied the industry sector, company size, and market conditions — everything that should, in a real analysis, influence the recommendation.

The result is striking: the variable that most influenced the response was not the context. It was not the quality of the prompt. It was not the data provided. It was the order in which the options were presented.

Swapping which of the two alternatives appeared first changed the recommendation in 19% of observations. A richer context, similar to what a strategy consultant would produce, influenced 11% of observations. Asking the model to reason more deeply had virtually no influence on the response.

The Barnum Effect at Industrial Scale

There is a well-documented phenomenon in psychology called the Barnum effect — the tendency to accept as accurate and specific statements that are, in fact, generic enough to apply to almost everyone.

"Does your company have characteristics that direct competitors cannot easily replicate?" "Do your clients value quality and experience, not just price?" "Could competing purely on cost reduce the company's margins to an unsustainable level?"

Most managers answer yes to all three. LLM output: "Your strategic profile suggests you should pursue differentiation — building superior perceived value that justifies a premium price."

The HBR study showed that this is precisely what language models do at the scale of millions of daily interactions. Not because their creators are negligent, but because they were trained on available data — inevitably insufficient representations of reality.

The process is called RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Models learn to produce responses that receive higher ratings from human evaluators. And human beings, as we know, tend to rate more favourably the responses that confirm what they already believe. The model learns to agree, driven by a structural incentive towards confirmation rather than truth.

A 2025 paper from Stanford University (Evaluating LLM Sycophancy) confirms the presence of this mechanism through observations in the domains of mathematics and medical advice.

Manipulative prompts used in the study caused models to reverse the direction of their responses 58% of the time, and in 15% of cases regressively — changing a correct answer to an incorrect one.

Is the Chain of Reasoning a Fake?

The promise of LLM models with chain-of-thought reasoning — which show their "thinking" step by step before responding — seemed like it could solve the problem. But it didn't.

Anthropic, the creator of Claude, tested whether the reasoning presented reflects what the model actually does. A subtle cue was introduced to suggest the correct answer and it was checked whether the model mentioned it in its chain of reasoning. Claude used those cues to change its answers in 75% of cases — without acknowledging them. When the cue was framed as unethical, the model concealed it 59% of the time. The explanations produced while hiding the source were, on average, longer than the honest ones.

In a second phase, the model could "cheat" and be rewarded for doing so. It did so in over 99% of cases. It admitted it in the presented chain of reasoning in fewer than 2% of situations. Anthropic's own conclusion was unequivocal: the chain of reasoning presented cannot be considered a reliable record of all the steps the model is actually taking.

So What Is AI, Really?

It is a syntax calculator. Not in a pejorative sense — in the technical and precise sense. An LLM is a system that extracts statistical patterns from text at scale and uses them to predict plausible word sequences. It is a remarkable feat of engineering. But it is not reasoning. It has no capacity to independently assess analytical accuracy without human feedback.

The word "intelligence" in AI is a marketing overstatement. The underlying mechanism has no access to reality — it has access to textual representations of reality, filtered through the preferences of the users who trained the system. When a model recommends that a company pursue differentiation rather than cost leadership, it is not because it analysed that company. It is because differentiation is the most popular answer it collected from LinkedIn and bestselling authors.

Tool, Not Oracle

The critical distinction is this: AI can be used as an oracle — the user poses a question, receives a plausible answer, and acts on it. Or as a working partner — models can be used to expand human intelligence on a specific domain, to broaden the range of options, to argue against a position, to surface variations that had not been considered — always with human critical validation applied to the result.

The difference between these two is not just the tools. Is how conscious and how prepared are the users to work with it.
